top_level_objectives: Understand how VSEPR theory predicts three-dimensional molecular geometry from Lewis structures
Recognize the five fundamental electron-domain geometries and how lone pairs modify them
Explain why electron domains arrange to minimize repulsion and how this determines bond angles
Connect VSEPR predictions to actual molecular structures of common compounds

scenes.brief_purpose: Establish the core principle of VSEPR theory: electron domains repel each other and arrange to minimize repulsion around a central atom.
key_visuals: Central atom (carbon or sulfur) surrounded by 4-6 repelling electron domain spheres that automatically push apart
Arrows or force vectors showing repulsive interactions between domains
Text label showing 'electron domain' definition (both bonding and lone pairs)
student_actions: Observe how domains repel and rearrange as the student adds more domains around the central atom
Manipulate the number of electron domains and predict where the next domain will position itself
Observe that the system settles into a minimum-repulsion arrangement automatically

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce and visualize the five fundamental three-dimensional arrangements of electron domains: linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral.
key_visuals: Five separate interactive models, each showing a central atom with 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6 electron domains arranged in their characteristic geometry
Bond angles labeled (180°, 120°, 109.5°, 90° and 120°, 90°)
Highlighted regions showing bond angles and domain positions
student_actions: Rotate and examine each of the five geometries from multiple angles
Identify bond angles in each geometry
Match each electron count (2 through 6) to its corresponding geometry
Predict the geometry for a new electron domain arrangement

scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate that lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, causing deviations from ideal bond angles and modifying molecular geometry.
key_visuals: Side-by-side comparison of bonding pairs and lone pairs, with lone pairs shown as larger or more diffuse electron clouds
A tetrahedral electron-domain geometry with one domain replaced by a lone pair, showing the repulsion pushing bonding pairs closer together
Bond angle measurements showing deviation (e.g., 109.5° ideal vs. actual bond angles in molecules with lone pairs)
student_actions: Observe the relative repulsion strength: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bonding pair > bonding pair–bonding pair
Replace bonding domains with lone pairs one at a time and measure the resulting bond angles
Predict how bond angles will change when lone pairs are added to a tetrahedral geometry

scenes.scene_name: Linear and Trigonal Planar Geometries with Lone Pairs
scenes.brief_purpose: Show how lone pairs modify the linear (2 domains) and trigonal planar (3 domains) electron-domain geometries.
key_visuals: Linear arrangement with 0, 1, and 2 lone pairs shown progressively (linear → linear, then what happens with a lone pair)
Trigonal planar arrangement with 0, 1, and 2 lone pairs (trigonal planar → bent → linear, or appropriate geometries)
Clear labeling of resulting molecular geometries (e.g., 'trigonal planar electron-domain geometry, bent molecular geometry')
student_actions: Add lone pairs to a 2-domain system and predict the resulting molecular geometry
Add lone pairs to a 3-domain system and observe the molecular geometry change from trigonal planar to bent
Identify the key molecular shape names (e.g., bent for 2 bonding + 1 lone pair)

scenes.scene_name: Tetrahedral and Trigonal Bipyramidal with Lone Pairs
scenes.brief_purpose: Explore how lone pairs modify tetrahedral (4 domains) and trigonal bipyramidal (5 domains) geometries, producing trigonal pyramidal, seesaw, T-shaped, and related shapes.
key_visuals: Tetrahedral electron-domain geometry with 0, 1, and 2 lone pairs shown, resulting in tetrahedral, trigonal pyramidal, and bent molecular geometries
Trigonal bipyramidal electron-domain geometry with 0, 1, 2, and 3 lone pairs shown, resulting in trigonal bipyramidal, seesaw, T-shaped, and linear molecular geometries
Axial vs. equatorial positions highlighted for trigonal bipyramidal to show why lone pairs prefer equatorial positions
Bond angles labeled in each case
student_actions: Manipulate lone pairs in a tetrahedral system and observe the molecular shape transformation
Explain why lone pairs in a trigonal bipyramidal system occupy equatorial positions (120° apart) rather than axial (90° from others)
Predict the molecular geometry for different combinations of bonding and lone pairs in tetrahedral and trigonal bipyramidal systems
Identify seesaw, T-shaped shapes as modifications of trigonal bipyramidal

scenes.brief_purpose: Show how lone pairs modify the octahedral electron-domain geometry (6 domains), producing square planar and square pyramidal shapes.
key_visuals: Octahedral electron-domain geometry with 0, 1, 2, and 3 lone pairs shown
Square pyramidal shape (4 bonding + 1 lone pair)
Square planar shape (4 bonding + 2 lone pairs opposite each other)
Equatorial and axial position labels explaining why opposite positions are preferred for lone pairs
student_actions: Add lone pairs to an octahedral system and observe the resulting molecular geometries
Explain why 2 lone pairs in octahedral are placed opposite each other to minimize repulsion
Predict whether a given octahedral arrangement will be square pyramidal or square planar

scenes.scene_name: Connecting VSEPR Predictions to Real Molecules
scenes.brief_purpose: Bridge theory to practice by showing Lewis structures of real molecules (water, ammonia, methane, PF5, SF6, XeF4) and comparing VSEPR predictions to observed three-dimensional structures.
key_visuals: Lewis structures displayed alongside 3D molecular models
Labels showing electron-domain count, electron-domain geometry, molecular geometry, and bond angles for each molecule
Real molecular geometries rendered as accurate 3D ball-and-stick or space-filling models
Bond angles marked and compared to ideal values (e.g., H–O–H in water = 104.5° vs. ideal tetrahedral 109.5°)
student_actions: For each molecule (H2O, NH3, CH4, PF5, SF6, XeF4), count the electron domains and predict the electron-domain and molecular geometries
Compare predictions to the observed 3D structures shown
Explain deviations from ideal bond angles based on lone-pair repulsion
Verify that VSEPR correctly predicts the shapes of all six example molecules

scenes.brief_purpose: Consolidate understanding by having students apply VSEPR to molecules they have not yet analyzed, demonstrating mastery of the theory.
key_visuals: A new molecule's Lewis structure displayed (e.g., H2S, CO2, PCl3, or similar)
Space for predicted geometry before revealing the actual 3D structure
Revealed 3D molecular structure after prediction
Comparison view showing electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry side-by-side
student_actions: Predict the electron-domain geometry, molecular geometry, and approximate bond angles for a new molecule based solely on its Lewis structure
Receive feedback showing the actual 3D structure and compare it to the prediction
Reflect on the accuracy of VSEPR theory and the importance of accounting for lone-pair repulsion
Optionally, solve 2–3 additional challenge molecules to build confidence
